lessons.title: Logical Thinking
lessons.introduction: Logical thinking breaks decisions into clear true/false conditions so your program behaves predictably in every situation.
objectives: Translate everyday rules into unambiguous true/false conditions.
Combine simple conditions with AND, OR, and NOT reasoning.
Identify edge cases before writing code.
conceptExplanation: Programming is applied logic. Before touching a keyboard, an engineer asks: under what exact condition should this motor run, and under what exact condition must it stop?
Ambiguous rules cause dangerous robot bugs. Logical thinking forces you to define both what happens when a condition is true AND what happens when it is false.
lessons.analogy: Think of a microwave oven door: the heater runs ONLY when the timer is greater than zero AND the door is closed. If either condition is false, heating stops immediately.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Logical rules evaluate conditions to true or false.
rules: Every condition must resolve cleanly to true or false.
Always check boundary values (e.g., exactly equal to the threshold).

codeExamples.title: Safe Motor Enable Logic
codeExamples.description: Checks both an enable switch and a clear obstacle flag before running a motor.

lineByLine.explanation: Represents whether the master safety switch is ON.
Requires BOTH conditions to be true before enabling motors.
Guarantees a safe halt state whenever either condition fails.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Industrial robotic arms use dual-condition safety interlocks so a machine never moves if a guard door is open.

commonMistakes.fix: Always ask: what should hardware do when the condition is NOT met?
Use AND (&&) when all safety rules must pass; use OR (||) when any single trigger is enough.

tryItYourself.title: m02_logic.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change pathClear to false and verify which message prints.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: With pathClear set to false, Serial Monitor prints STOP.

exercises.prompt: A robot should move ONLY if batteryOk is true AND obstacleDetected is false. Which condition matches?
exercises.explanation: && requires both parts to be true, and ! negates obstacleDetected so it is true when no obstacle is present.

exercises.prompt: Complete the logical AND operator so both checks must be true.

summary: Logical thinking turns vague ideas into exact true/false rules.
Always handle both true and false outcomes.
Safety interlocks commonly use logical AND (&&).

lessons.title: Problem Decomposition
lessons.introduction: Problem decomposition splits one intimidating robotics project into small, independent sub-problems you can build and test one at a time.
objectives: Break a multi-part robotics task into independent sub-tasks.
Test each sub-task in isolation before combining them.
Reduce debugging time by isolating hardware and logic components.
conceptExplanation: Beginners often try to wire five sensors and write 150 lines of code all at once — and when nothing works, they have no idea where the bug is.

Decomposition solves this: an 'Automatic Smart Plant Waterer' splits into (1) read soil moisture sensor, (2) decide if soil is dry, (3) turn pump relay on for 3 seconds, and (4) wait before re-checking.
lessons.analogy: You don't build a car in one single mold — you build and test the brakes, steering, engine, and headlights separately, then assemble them.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Map each sub-problem to its own dedicated function.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
int readMoisture();          // Sub-problem 1
bool isTooDry(int reading);  // Sub-problem 2
void runPump(int seconds);   // Sub-problem 3
rules: Each sub-problem should have one clear job.
Verify each piece in isolation with Serial Monitor before combining.

codeExamples.title: Decomposed Streetlight Logic
codeExamples.description: Splits reading light and controlling the lamp into two clear helper functions.

lineByLine.explanation: Isolates sensor reading into one reusable function.
Isolates actuator output into a second function.
Connects the two pieces cleanly inside loop().

lessons.realWorldApplication: Autonomous drones decompose flight into separate modules: sensor fusion, altitude hold, motor mixing, and radio telemetry.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing one giant loop() with everything mixed together
commonMistakes.fix: Split sensing, decision making, and actuation into small named functions.
Verify each sensor alone via Serial Monitor first.

tryItYourself.title: m02_decomposition.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a Serial.println(level); inside loop() to inspect the sensor sub-problem.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor displays live light readings while the lamp responds whenever the reading drops below 350.

exercises.prompt: What is the main advantage of problem decomposition before wiring and coding?
options: Each small sub-task can be built, tested, and debugged independently.
It eliminates the need for setup() in Arduino.
It makes the microcontroller run at double clock speed.
It removes the need for resistors.
exercises.explanation: Isolating sub-problems prevents cascading bugs and makes hardware troubleshooting straightforward.

exercises.prompt: Order the decomposed steps for an ultrasonic obstacle-avoiding robot.
shuffledSteps: Command motors to turn or drive
correctOrder: Command motors to turn or drive
exercises.explanation: Sense first, decide second, act third.

summary: Decomposition breaks complex projects into small, testable parts.
Test each sensor and actuator independently before integrating.
Map each sub-task to its own clean function.

lessons.title: Algorithms
lessons.introduction: An algorithm is a finite, well-ordered sequence of steps that transforms inputs into a desired outcome.
objectives: Define what makes a set of steps a valid algorithm.
Design a clear step-by-step algorithm for a traffic light controller.
Trace an algorithm by hand to catch logic flaws early.
conceptExplanation: Before writing a single semicolon of C++, you design the algorithm. An algorithm is language-independent: the same traffic-light algorithm works in C++, Python, or on a whiteboard.
Good algorithms are finite (each cycle completes), unambiguous (no guesswork), and handle every possible input state.
lessons.analogy: An algorithm is like turn-by-turn GPS navigation: each step is unambiguous, ordered, and leads reliably from start to destination.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Write numbered steps before translating them into C++.
rules: Every step should describe one concrete action or decision.
Check that no state leaves an old output accidentally stuck ON.

codeExamples.title: Traffic Light Algorithm in Code
codeExamples.description: Direct translation of the 3-step traffic light algorithm.

lineByLine.explanation: Step 1: Activates Green while guaranteeing Red and Yellow are OFF.
Holds the Green state for 4 seconds.
Step 2: Transitions cleanly to Yellow.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Path-planning algorithms, PID motor controllers, and sorting machines all start as clear algorithmic steps before becoming code.

commonMistakes.mistake: Jumping straight into coding without an algorithm
commonMistakes.fix: Write a 4-line numbered plan first; it prevents tangled if-else spaghetti.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving previous LEDs ON during transitions
commonMistakes.fix: Explicitly turn off the previous state when entering the next state.

tryItYourself.title: m02_algorithm.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Shorten the delays to 1000, 500, and 1000 ms for fast bench testing.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Three LEDs on pins 8, 9, and 10 cycle cleanly Green -> Yellow -> Red.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best describes an algorithm?
options: A clear, ordered sequence of steps that solves a problem regardless of programming language.
A special Arduino library you download from the internet.
exercises.explanation: Algorithms are language-independent step-by-step plans for solving problems.

exercises.prompt: In a 3-LED traffic light, when Yellow turns HIGH, Green should be set to ___1___.
exercises.explanation: Turning Green LOW ensures only Yellow is active during the caution phase.

summary: An algorithm is an ordered, unambiguous plan to solve a problem.
Design the algorithm first, then translate it to C++.
Explicitly manage transitions between states.

lessons.title: Pseudocode
lessons.introduction: Pseudocode is structured plain English that looks like code so you can verify logic without worrying about semicolons or syntax rules.
objectives: Write clean pseudocode using IF, ELSE, REPEAT, and SET.
Convert pseudocode line-by-line into valid Arduino C++.
Use pseudocode to communicate logic clearly with teammates.
conceptExplanation: Pseudocode sits halfway between human language and C++. Because there is no strict compiler checking it, you can focus 100% on whether your logic actually works.
Once your pseudocode reads cleanly, translating each line into Arduino C++ becomes straightforward and low-stress.
lessons.analogy: Pseudocode is like a rough pencil sketch before painting with ink — fast to erase, easy to adjust, and prevents costly rework.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Use uppercase keywords (SET, READ, IF, ELSE, REPEAT) with indentation.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
READ lightValue FROM A0
IF lightValue < 400 THEN
  TURN streetlight ON
ELSE
  TURN streetlight OFF
rules: Keep one logical action per line.
Indent steps inside IF and REPEAT blocks just like real code.

codeExamples.title: Pseudocode Translated to Arduino C++
codeExamples.description: Side-by-side translation of a temperature fan controller.

lineByLine.explanation: Represents the READ tempC pseudocode step.
Directly matches IF tempC >= 30 THEN.
Directly matches ELSE TURN fan OFF.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Robotics teams write pseudocode on whiteboards during competitions so mechanical and software members agree on robot behavior before coding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making pseudocode too vague (e.g., 'do robot stuff')
commonMistakes.fix: Specify exact inputs, conditions, and outputs.
5 lines of pseudocode saves 30 minutes of debugging nested ifs.

tryItYourself.title: m02_pseudocode.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change the threshold from 30 to 28 and add Serial.println("Fan ON") inside the if branch.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pin 6 goes HIGH and Serial Monitor prints 'Fan ON' when tempC meets the threshold.

exercises.prompt: Why is pseudocode valuable for beginners?
options: It lets you design and verify logic without getting blocked by C++ syntax rules.
Arduino IDE compiles pseudocode directly into machine code.
It replaces the need to test on hardware.
exercises.explanation: Pseudocode separates logical problem-solving from syntax memorization.

exercises.prompt: Which C++ line correctly translates: IF distance < 20 THEN stopMotors?
exercises.explanation: C++ requires parentheses around the condition and braces around the body, with () to call a function.

summary: Pseudocode expresses program logic in structured plain English.
Use indentation and clear keywords like IF, ELSE, and REPEAT.
Translate verified pseudocode line-by-line into C++.

lessons.title: Flowcharts
lessons.introduction: Flowcharts visualize program flow using standard shapes so you can see every branch and loop at a glance.
objectives: Recognize standard flowchart symbols: Oval (Start/End), Rectangle (Process), Diamond (Decision), Arrows (Flow).
Read a sensor-decision flowchart and trace both YES and NO branches.
Convert a flowchart directly into Arduino if/else code.
conceptExplanation: Some bugs are invisible in text but obvious in a diagram. Flowcharts use standardized shapes: rounded ovals for Start/End, rectangles for actions/processes, and diamonds for true/false decisions.
Every decision diamond must have two labeled outgoing arrows (YES/True and NO/False). Tracing arrows reveals dead ends or missing branches before you write code.
lessons.analogy: A flowchart is a subway map for your program — you can trace every possible route a signal can take.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Each flowchart diamond becomes an if/else statement in C++.
rules: Oval = Start/End; Rectangle = Action; Diamond = Decision.
Every arrow must lead somewhere — avoid dangling branches.

codeExamples.title: Flowchart to Streetlight Code
codeExamples.description: Directly implements the automatic streetlight flowchart diagram shown above.

lineByLine.explanation: Matches the Rectangle step: Read Light Sensor.
Matches the Decision Diamond: val < 400?
Matches the YES and NO action rectangles.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Embedded engineers include flowcharts in design reviews for safety-critical systems like battery management and autonomous braking.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving a decision diamond with only one arrow
commonMistakes.fix: Always draw both YES and NO paths.
Remember Arduino's loop() returns to the top after finishing the bottom step.

tryItYourself.title: m02_flowchart.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Update the decision threshold from 400 to 500.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pin 9 turns HIGH whenever A0 reads below 500 and LOW at 500 or above.

exercises.prompt: Which flowchart shape represents a Yes/No decision (such as an if statement)?
exercises.explanation: A diamond represents a branching decision with True/False (Yes/No) outgoing paths.

exercises.prompt: What does a rectangle represent in a standard flowchart?
options: A process or action step (e.g., read sensor or turn LED on)
The start of the program only
exercises.explanation: Rectangles represent concrete processing or action steps.

summary: Flowcharts visualize control flow with standard shapes.
Diamonds represent decisions with both YES and NO paths.
Every flowchart maps cleanly into C++ statements.

diagram.caption: Standard flowchart showing sensor reading, decision diamond, and YES/NO output actions.

lessons.title: Input, Processing, and Output (IPO)
lessons.introduction: Every embedded system — from a thermostat to a Mars rover — follows the Input-Processing-Output (IPO) model.
objectives: Classify components as Inputs (sensors), Processing (microcontroller logic), or Outputs (actuators).
Structure Arduino sketches cleanly around the IPO cycle.
Trace data as it flows from physical world to code and back to physical world.
conceptExplanation: Input collects information from the outside world (push buttons, photoresistors, ultrasonic sensors). Processing uses C++ variables, math, and decisions inside the microcontroller to interpret that data. Output drives physical actuators (LEDs, buzzers, servos, motors) or displays.
Organizing loop() in strict IPO order — Read Inputs, Process Logic, Write Outputs — makes even complex robotics code clean and predictable.
lessons.analogy: Your own body uses IPO constantly: eyes see a red traffic light (Input), brain decides to brake (Processing), foot presses the pedal (Output).

syntaxExplanation.summary: Structure loop() in three clear phases: Input -> Process -> Output.
rules: Read all needed sensors at the top of loop().
Perform calculations and decisions in the middle.
Drive LEDs, servos, motors, or Serial at the bottom.

codeExamples.title: Clean IPO Dimmer Sketch
codeExamples.description: Reads a potentiometer (Input), scales it (Process), and drives LED brightness (Output).

lineByLine.explanation: INPUT: Reads 0–1023 from the analog knob.
PROCESS: Converts the 10-bit reading to an 8-bit PWM brightness.
OUTPUT: Sets the LED brightness on PWM pin 9.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Line-following robots run an IPO loop hundreds of times per second: read IR array (Input) -> compute steering error (Process) -> set left/right motor speeds (Output).

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing sensor reads randomly inside motor code
commonMistakes.fix: Group reads at the start of loop() for consistent snapshots.
Always check input range (0–1023 on Uno) vs output range (0–255 for analogWrite).

tryItYourself.title: m02_ipo.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Reverse the map() output range from (0, 255) to (255, 0) so turning the knob dims the LED instead.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Reversing map() makes brightness decrease as the potentiometer turns up.

exercises.prompt: In the IPO model, what category does an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor belong to?
exercises.explanation: Sensors gather physical measurements from the environment, making them Inputs.

exercises.prompt: Which component is an Output actuator?
exercises.explanation: A servo motor converts electrical signals into physical motion, making it an Output.

summary: Every robotics system follows Input -> Processing -> Output.
Structuring loop() in IPO order keeps code clean and bug-resistant.
Sensors are Inputs; C++ logic is Processing; LEDs/motors/buzzers are Outputs.

diagram.caption: The Input-Process-Output (IPO) architecture at the heart of every Arduino project.

lessons.title: Designing Solutions Before Coding
lessons.introduction: Five minutes of planning on paper prevents hours of trial-and-error debugging at the workbench.
objectives: Write a 4-part mini design sheet: Goal, Pin Map, IPO Plan, and Edge Cases.
Check pin conflicts before wiring a breadboard.
Translate a finished design sheet directly into clean Arduino C++.
conceptExplanation: Experienced engineers rarely open Arduino IDE with a blank mind. First, they list every connected part and its assigned pin (the Pin Map), write the IPO flow in pseudocode, and list edge cases (what if a sensor disconnects or times out?).
This habit is what separates independent programmers from people stuck copying random sketches off the internet.
lessons.analogy: No carpenter cuts expensive lumber without measuring and marking pencil lines first. Your pin map and pseudocode are your pencil lines.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Document your Pin Map as const int declarations at the top of your sketch.
rules: Assign every component a unique pin (avoid D0/D1 on Uno when using Serial).
Confirm PWM (~) pins for analogWrite() and analog pins (A0+) for analogRead().
List at least one safety/edge case before coding.

codeExamples.title: Design-First Buzzer Alert
codeExamples.description: Starts with a clear pin map and IPO comment header before setup() and loop().

lineByLine.explanation: Translates the paper pin map into named constants.
Clear processing step turning LOW active button into a readable boolean.
Cleanly drives and silences the buzzer output.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Before building any competition robot, teams maintain a Pin Assignment Table so wiring and software never collide on the same GPIO.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assigning two devices to the same pin
commonMistakes.fix: Keep a Pin Map at the top of every sketch so every pin is visible in one place.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using D0 or D1 on Uno for buttons while using Serial
commonMistakes.fix: Pins 0 and 1 carry USB Serial on Uno R3/Nano Classic — keep them free for debugging.

tryItYourself.title: m02_design_first.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change the buzzer frequency from 1000 Hz to 1500 Hz.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pressing the button lights pin 8 and plays a higher-pitched 1500 Hz tone on pin 6; releasing stops both.

exercises.prompt: Why should you avoid connecting buttons or LEDs to pins 0 and 1 on an Arduino Uno R3 when using Serial Monitor?
options: Pins 0 (RX) and 1 (TX) are shared with USB Serial communication and uploading.
Pins 0 and 1 do not support digitalWrite.
Pins 0 and 1 only work with servo motors.
exercises.explanation: Using D0/D1 on Uno R3 interferes with USB Serial Monitor output and can block sketch uploads.

exercises.prompt: Write a const int pin map declaring TRIG_PIN as 9 and ECHO_PIN as 10.
exercises.sampleSolution:
const int TRIG_PIN = 9;
const int ECHO_PIN = 10;
exercises.explanation: Named constants at the top of a sketch act as a live pin map.

summary: Plan Goal, Pin Map, IPO logic, and Edge Cases before coding.
Store your pin map as const int declarations at the top of the sketch.
Avoid pin conflicts (especially D0/D1 on Uno R3).
